It feeds upon the soil itself, and having eaten its way through a whole mountain it lies down to sleep and to grow. Born deep underground, it becomes a pupa once it has swallowed earth enough to raise a hill.
The miners who break into its sleeping-chamber tread softly and go another way, for they have no wish to be under the mountain when it wakes.

247.notes:
Its shell is hard as sheet rock and its body harder still, and its blind thrashing within is strong enough to topple a mountainside. It will not hold still even in the pupa, and already it has arms and legs formed beneath the solid casing.
The ground shudders where a Pupitar rages in its shell, and whole slopes have come down for the fury of a creature that cannot yet see the sky.

248.notes:
No manner of blow can harm its armored body, and knowing this it is quick and eager to make challenge of anything that crosses it. In a single one of its mighty hands it holds the power to shake the ground and bring the mountains down.
It topples cliffs for the sport of testing its strength, and reshapes the very hills of its country in its restlessness. The land remembers where a Tyranitar has walked.

249.notes:
It keeps to the deep bottom of the sea and stirs but seldom, for its powers are held to be too great to loose upon the world without cause. It is said to have the gift of calming the wildest storm, and to show itself only when the storms are at their worst.
Sailors caught in a tempest pray for a glimpse of its wings against the black cloud, for where Lugia rises, the sea is said to fall quiet.
249.scribe: Guardian of the sea and of the tower by the water. It is spoken of in a whisper, and seen by fewer still.

250.notes:
It flies the skies of the world without ceasing upon seven-colored wings, and where its shadow passes it is said to leave a rainbow in the air behind it. It will show itself, the old belief holds, only to a trainer whose heart is truly pure.
It is bound in every tale to the burned tower at Ecruteak, and to the three beasts said to have risen from its fire, and the faithful climb the tower still in hope of the shine of its wings.
250.scribe: Guardian of the sky and of the burned tower. Legend gives it the raising of the three roused beasts.

251.notes:
It wanders freely across time itself, and in whatever age it alights the grass and the trees of the forest spring up green and glad. Revered as the warden of the wood, it appears wherever a forest grows fair and unspoiled.
Where a Celebi has walked, the barren places bloom, and the foresters plant a sapling at any spot where the old stories say it once was seen.
251.scribe: A creature of the forest and of time. The last folio of the second kingdom, as Mew closed the first.

252.notes:
Small hooks upon the soles of its feet let it climb a sheer wall as easily as level ground, and it strikes at a foe with a swing of its thick tail. It keeps to the trees and watches the forest floor from above.
It is a cool-headed little creature, and shows no fear before a larger beast, sizing up its chances with a steady eye.
252.scribe: The first creature of the third kingdom, and a starter's companion in the manner of Bulbasaur and Chikorita before it.

253.notes:
The leaves that sprout along its body serve to hide it among the forest green, and it slips from branch to branch too swiftly for the eye to follow. It fells its prey and is gone before the deed is marked.
It lives in the deep wood and comes down to the ground but seldom, moving always through the high canopy.

254.notes:
The leaves upon its arms are edged like blades, and it springs about the branches with a speed that leaves only a green blur behind it. In the treetops it has no equal for agility.
It guards its patch of forest jealously, and rouses the whole canopy to answer any intruder that dares the trees it calls its own.

255.notes:
A small downy chick that follows close at its keeper's heel with unsteady steps, and for all its meekness it breathes a fire hotter than any forge. When it is content, a gentle warmth rises from it.
Kept by the hearth it needs no other fire, and it cheeps mournfully when its keeper strays out of sight.

256.notes:
It hardens its legs and thighs by running the fields and the mountains, and those legs hold both speed and a fearsome kick. The flame at its brow flares brighter as its training tells.
It spars against anything it can find, and a keeper must set it strong tasks or it will pick its own, to the ruin of the furniture.

257.notes:
Fire spouts from its wrists and wreathes its knuckles, so that its every blow lands with a scorching, and its punches sear whatever they strike. It leaps buildings in a single bound to fall upon a foe.
The fighting-schools of Hoenn hold it among the fiercest of strikers, and its bearing in the ring is that of a champion who knows it.

258.notes:
The fin upon its head is a keen sort of radar, and by it the little creature reads the least stir of water or air about it, so that nothing comes upon it unawares. It sleeps buried in the streambed with only that fin showing.
It is strong past its size, and will heave aside a stone many times its own weight to reach a morsel beneath.

259.notes:
A thin and sticky film covers its skin and lets it live out of the water and upon the land, where it plays in the mud of the riverbank. It sees poorly in the murk it loves, and trusts to touch instead.
It is happiest half-sunk in a marsh, and a keeper who would keep one must resign the garden to the mire.

260.notes:
It is very strong, strong enough to drag a boulder of more than a ton without labor, and its broad arms make short work of any obstacle. It swims the flood and walks the mud with equal ease.
When the storms come and the rivers rise, it is said to plant itself before the villages and break the force of the water, and the marsh-folk honor it for it.

261.notes:
At first sight it bites at anything that moves, and once it has fixed on a quarry it runs the creature down without pause until the chase is spent. It is bolder in a pack than alone.
For all its snapping it is a coward at heart, and a firm hand and a steady voice will teach it loyalty in time.

262.notes:
It hunts in a disciplined pack, running its prey to ground with a patient cruelty, and it will never once disobey a keeper it has come to respect. Wild, it answers only to the leader of the pack.
The herders of Hoenn prize a well-schooled Mightyena above a fence, for it turns back the raiders that a fence never could.

263.notes:
It wanders here and there without rest, forever crossing its own path, for it is possessed of a boundless curiosity and must investigate all it meets. Its coat runs in a jagged pattern of light and dark.
It turns aside for every small novelty, and a keeper who takes one walking must be content to go wherever its nose leads.

264.notes:
It runs always at full tilt and only ever in a straight line, so that to change its course it must stop and make a sharp right angle before dashing off anew. It cannot round a corner at speed to save its life.
It is a swift hunter of small things in the undergrowth, though it charges headlong into any wall that stands athwart its path.

265.notes:
With the spikes upon its tail it strips the bark from trees and drinks the sap that wells out. Which of two forms it will take is written already in the color of it, though none can read the sign until the change is upon it.
It spins its silk when its growing is done, and the cocoon it makes betrays nothing of what will hatch from it.

266.notes:
It fastens itself to a branch by a thread of silk and hangs there quietly, waiting out its change, its hard shell turned to catch the light. It stirs but little, husbanding its strength.
Within, the wings of a fair creature are forming, and the country children watch the pale cocoons for the day they split.

267.notes:
Its favorite food is the sweet pollen of flowers, and to see one it is enough to set a potted bloom upon the sill and wait. It drifts from blossom to blossom on broad and gaudy wings.
It is drawn to bright colors above all, and a garden in flower will bring a whole flight of them by noon.

268.notes:
It wraps itself wholly in a fine silk spun from its mouth, and once the silk has closed over its eyes it does not stir again until its change is done. It endures whatever befalls it in patience.
Its cocoon is the near twin of its cousin's, and only the practiced eye can guess which fair or foul thing waits within.

269.notes:
It is drawn without fail toward light, and swarms of it gather at the bright lamps of the towns, where they are counted a plague upon the streetlamps. The powder of its wings carries a poison.
The lamplighters of Hoenn curse its coming, and net whole clouds of it from about the town lanterns of a summer night.

270.notes:
It floats upon the still surface of ponds and lakes, and grows weak and ails if the broad leaf upon its back should wither. It drifts where the water carries it, seeming half a plant itself.
Small creatures ride across the pond upon its leaf, and the country folk take a floating Lotad for a sign of clean and healthy water.

271.notes:
It stirs only after dusk, and a mischief-maker it is, given to startling anglers by tugging at their lines from below. It keeps its slick skin ever moist and delights in the rain.
It dances a slow and comic dance in the shallows by moonlight, and the water-folk are half fond of the rogue for all its tricks.

272.notes:
The moment it hears a merry, festive tune it begins to dance, and its dancing is said to bring on the rains that swell the harvest. It is a carefree and a joyous creature.
The farmers of the dry season play music at the pond's edge to set the Ludicolo dancing, and swear the clouds gather to the beat.

273.notes:
It fixes the crown of its head to a tree branch and hangs there drawing moisture from the wood, still and quiet as a true acorn. It stirs but rarely, and then only to find a better bough.
The woodsmen have gathered what they took for acorns and been startled to find them blink, and now they look twice before they fill the basket.

274.notes:
It lives in the deep overgrown forest and ventures out now and again for no better reason than to startle passing folk. It plays upon a leaf-whistle a tune that carries eerily through the trees.
Travelers who hear that thin piping in the dusk hurry their steps, though the creature means no worse than mischief by it.

275.notes:
It is a mysterious thing, said to dwell atop towering trees a thousand years old and more, and it is held to summon the winds. When it spreads the great fans of its hands, a gale rises out of a still evening.
The old foresters will not fell a thousand-year tree for fear of what may keep its house at the crown, and leave the eldest giants standing out of a wary respect.

276.notes:
It stands its ground against any foe however strong, and will not give way though plainly overmatched, for its heart is bolder than its small body. It defends its patch with a furious courage.
A single Taillow has been seen to drive off a beast ten times its size by sheer effrontery, and the country folk cheer the pluck of it.

277.notes:
It wheels high overhead in graceful arcs, then folds its wings and stoops at a steep angle the moment it marks its prey below. It keeps its glossy feathers meticulously preened, for a ragged wing spoils its dive.
It is a proud and splendid flier, and the falconers of Hoenn count a well-kept Swellow the finest bird in the three kingdoms.

278.notes:
It has the habit of carrying off prey and bright trinkets in its beak and hiding them away in all manner of secret places. It rides the sea-wind on stiff white wings.
Sailors leave nothing shiny on the deck when Wingull wheel about the mast, for what they filch is seldom seen again.

279.notes:
Its vast bill serves it as a carrier, and within it the great bird bears small creatures and eggs safely from place to place. It builds its nest upon a sheer sea-cliff.
The fisher-folk of the coast are said to send messages and even passengers by Pelipper in foul weather, when no boat dares the water.

280.notes:
By the horns upon its head it feels the moods of the people near it, and it shows itself before them but rarely, keeping to hiding when their hearts are troubled. It draws near only to the gentle and the glad.
Where a Ralts creeps out to sit beside a stranger, the country folk take it as sure proof that the stranger is kind.

281.notes:
It is said that a Kirlia raised amid its keeper's happiness grows the more beautiful for it, and it dances of its own accord when its keeper is glad. It turns and spins upon the points of its feet.
It shares in the feelings of those it loves, dancing in their joy and drooping in their sorrow, and a keeper learns to guard his own moods for the creature's sake.

282.notes:
For a keeper to whom it has bound itself it will loose the full force of its mind, and there is said to be no power it will not spend to shield one it loves. It creates a small warp in space to turn aside a mortal blow.
The old tales hold that a Gardevoir will give its very life to save its keeper, and folk who have been so saved keep the day of it as holy ever after.

283.notes:
From the tips of its feet it seeps an oil that lets it skate upon the surface of the water without breaking it, and it darts across a pond as though the water were ice. It feeds on the small things of the shallows.
It leaves a faint bright film upon the water where it has passed, and children follow the trails of it across the millpond.

284.notes:
The great false eyes upon its antennae serve to cow a foe, so that a small creature seems to glare back with a fierce and watching face. It flaps its four wings to hover and to steer with ease.
It cannot abide the rain, which weighs its wings, and shelters under a broad leaf until the shower is past.

285.notes:
It dwells in the damp soil of the dark forest depths, and lies still beneath the fallen leaves where it is easily overlooked. It looses a bitter spore that turns the stomach of any that would eat it.
Foragers who mistake it for a true mushroom learn the difference in short and unhappy order, and thereafter tread the leaf-litter with care.

286.notes:
It closes upon a foe with a light and springing step, then strikes with long arms that stretch out further than any would guess, and the seeds upon it burst with a poison. Its footwork is quick past the following of the eye.
The fighting-schools study its dancing tread as they study the fencers', and count its stretching blows among the hardest to guard against.

287.notes:
It lolls about for better than twenty hours of every day, and moves so little that it needs scarcely any food to sustain it. It hangs from a branch and stirs only when it must.
It seems the very picture of idleness, yet the naturalists note that its heart is merely slow, not weak, and that great strength sleeps within the sloth.

288.notes:
It is forever itching and agitated to be up and rampaging, and cannot abide to sit still even a moment together. Its restlessness is the exact opposite of the form it springs from and the form it becomes.
Caged, it beats upon the bars in a fury, and it must be given room to run or it will do itself a mischief.
288.scribe: Between the two idle forms of its line stands this one, which cannot rest at all. The naturalists have never explained the middle temper.

289.notes:
It spends the whole day lying down and lolling about, and eats the grass within reach of it until that grass is gone, whereupon it grudgingly shifts to a fresh patch. For all its sloth it is enormously strong.
Roused to anger it is a terror, but it is roused only with great difficulty, and mostly it is content to lie and watch the clouds go over.

290.notes:
It lives underground for many years in utter darkness, drawing its nourishment from the roots of trees, and its eyes are near useless in the black earth. It readies itself slowly for the change to come.
When at last it climbs to the surface and sheds its skin, it leaves the empty husk behind, and thereby hangs a strange tale, as the next entries will tell.

291.notes:
It moves so swiftly that it cannot be seen at all, though its crying is heard plainly from the empty air, and for that the country folk half believe it a spirit. It circles a foe in a blur of sound.
It bursts from the ground at the moment of its change and is gone in an instant, leaving only its cry hanging behind it and its cast shell standing in the earth.

292.notes:
Its hard body does not move, not so much as a twitch, and when one looks within the shell there is found to be nothing there at all. It is held to be the empty husk that Ninjask left behind, given a strange half-life of its own.
It floats without breath or heartbeat, and the superstitious will not look long into the hole in its back, for they say a soul may be drawn out through it.
292.scribe: Born of the cast skin of Nincada at the moment Ninjask emerged: one creature shed into two. The scribes have puzzled long over how to number a thing that is a leaving-behind.

293.notes:
Its voice is commonly so faint as to be barely heard even by one who listens close, yet when it is startled or afraid it looses a cry that carries a great way. It covers its own ears against its own noise.
A sleeping Whismur is a gentle neighbor, but wake one unkindly and the whole street will know of it before the echo dies.

294.notes:
Its bellowing can shake a timber house to splinters, and it uses that voice to punish and to drive off any that trouble it. The round ports upon its cheeks swell as it draws breath to roar.
The townsfolk of Hoenn set a bellowing Loudred to break up rock in the quarries, and stop their ears with wax while it works.

295.notes:
Its bellow is loud enough to set the ground trembling, and when it draws breath through the ports of its body and looses it again, the very earth quakes. It is the loudest creature in all three kingdoms.
Whole villages have felt the tremor of an angered Exploud, and the wise measure their words when one is near, lest they be the cause of the next.

296.notes:
It is tenacious past all reason, and however many times it is knocked flat it rises and comes on again, until at last the foe wearies of felling it. Each hard fall, it seems, only toughens it the more.
The fighting-masters set their pupils to watch it, not for its skill, which is small, but for its refusal ever to stay down, which is a lesson worth more than any blow.

297.notes:
It practices its open-handed slaps wherever it finds room, against posts and cliffs and the trunks of trees, until that broad palm strikes with the force of a falling gate. It stamps and sweeps the ring before a bout.
One slap of a Hariyama has been known to lay a strong man flat, and the crowds that gather to its matches keep well back of the ropes.

298.notes:
It swings its great tail about like a lasso and hurls it out, and the force of the throw carries its own small round body flying after. The tip of the tail holds an oil lighter than water, and by it the little one floats and does not drown.
It is a droll sight to watch one fling its tail and be dragged after it across the shallows, blinking in surprise each time.
298.scribe: The infant form of Johto's Marill (No. 183), catalogued at last now that the third kingdom is opened.

299.notes:
The magnetic nose of it points forever to the north and will not be turned aside, so that two of them meeting cannot bring their faces together however they try. It sits still for long ages, drawing power from the earth.
The surveyors of Hoenn carried a Nosepass in place of a lodestone, and never lost their bearing, though they complained the creature would face but one way.

300.notes:
It is seized by a fascination for anything that moves and gives chase to it around and around, its own tail not least among the quarries. It tires itself out at the game and drops asleep where it stops.
It is a merry and affectionate creature, and a household that keeps one is never without entertainment, nor without a knocked-over cup or two.

301.notes:
It prefers to live free and unfettered, doing as it pleases at its own leisurely pace, and it makes its bed wherever the mood takes it rather than keep to one nest. It comes and goes as a guest, not a servant.
A keeper who would win a Delcatty must court it with patience and let it believe the whole arrangement was its own idea.

302.notes:
It leads a quiet life deep within the caverns, and it is feared for the old belief that it feeds upon the spirits of those it meets in the dark. The gems set in its body gleam faintly in the black.
Miners who see those two glinting stones watching from a side-passage turn back the way they came, and count the day's ore well lost.

303.notes:
The vast jaws that sprout from the back of its head are in truth steel horns transformed, and its meek and pretty face serves only to lull a foe into carelessness before those jaws snap shut. It seems harmless until the very last.
The wise do not trust the demure look of it, for the second face knows nothing of manners, and it is that face one meets in a quarrel.

304.notes:
Its body is made of steel, and to build that body it feeds upon the iron ore it digs from the mountainsides, cropping the metal as a beast crops grass. It is small but wondrously hard.
The miners of Hoenn grumble that an Aron will strip a fresh seam bare overnight, and they have learned to wall their diggings against the little iron-eaters.

305.notes:
It tempers its steel body by drinking deep of the mineral springs until it is bloated with the nourishing water, and it does battle by knocking its iron flanks together with a clangor. It grows heavy and hard with the years.
When two Lairon dispute a spring, the ringing of their collisions carries down the whole valley, and the villagers know to wait until the clangor stops before they draw their water.

306.notes:
It claims a whole mountain for its own and beats without mercy upon anything that trespasses on its ground. Its iron hide turns aside near any blow, and its two great horns can topple a rockface.
Yet the naturalists note that it tends its mountain as much as it guards it, replanting the slopes it has stripped, so that its tyranny leaves the land the richer in the end.

307.notes:
It undertakes a stern training of the mind deep in the mountains, and whenever it sits to meditate it folds its legs one upon the other and floats a little way off the ground. It eats but one berry a day, and needs no more.
Hermits of the high places keep company with it, and say a Meditite at its meditation is the stillest thing in the world save the stone it sits upon.

308.notes:
Through long meditation it kindles the energy within itself and sharpens a sixth sense past the common five, so that it seems to know a blow before it is thrown. It fights with a serene and dancing grace.
It reads a foe's intent in the set of the shoulders and is gone from the spot before the strike arrives, and the baffled challenger swings at empty air.

309.notes:
It stores lightning in the long hair of its coat, and stirs its own leg muscles with small charges to spur itself to greater speed. It races the storm and seems to gather strength from it.
It bristles and crackles before a thunderstorm, and the herders bring their beasts to shelter when they see a Electrike's coat stand out about it.

310.notes:
It discharges lightning without cease from its mane, and the sparks of it have been known to kindle forest fires in the dry season. It calls the storm down and rides the wind before it.
The country folk clear the brush about their homes when Manectric range the hills, for a single stray spark from its mane may set the whole slope alight.

311.notes:
It plays the cheerleader for its fellows, and whenever a companion strives well in a contest it bursts the sparks from the flowers of its hands in a shower of glad light. It draws its power from the joy of the crowd.
It is happiest in a pair with its cousin Minun, and the two together light up a festival better than any lantern.

312.notes:
It cares more for the cheering of its fellows than for its own safety, and will short out the lightning in its own body to shield a companion from harm. When its friend is downcast, it glows the brighter to hearten it.
Where Plusle burns bright in triumph, Minun burns bright in adversity, and the pair are never willingly parted.

313.notes:
With the coming of night it lights the lamp of its tail, and speaks to its fellows by quickening and dimming that glow in a language of light. It is drawn to the sweet scent that its mate gives off.
A summer meadow full of signalling Volbeat is one of the fairer sights of Hoenn, and lovers walk out to watch the lights answer one another in the dark.

314.notes:
It gives off a sweet fragrance that draws a swarm of Volbeat to it, and once they are gathered it leads their dancing lights this way and that across the night. It conducts the glowing throng as a leader conducts a choir.
The patterns it traces with its borrowed lights are said by the country folk to spell out messages, though none has ever learned to read them.

315.notes:
It looses the sharp thorns of its arms as darts against any that would steal the flowers it bears, and the sweet scent of those flowers belies the poison in the thorns. The redder the bloom, the stronger the venom.
Gardeners covet its flowers and rue its thorns in equal measure, and gather the blooms, when they dare, with a thick glove and a quick hand.
315.scribe: In later ages it was found to have both a babe before it and a further form beyond, but those belong to kingdoms this codex does not reach.

316.notes:
It has but a small heart and a smaller brain, and its stomach makes up the most of it, filled with juices that will dissolve near anything it swallows. It gulps down whatever it can fit and asks no questions.
It is not particular in its eating, and the townsfolk set one by the midden to be rid of what they would rather not carry off themselves.

317.notes:
When it marks its prey it spurts a hideously toxic fluid from its pores and drenches the creature, then waits at leisure for the venom to do its work. Its body is a single great bag of poison.
It swallows things whole that no other creature would dare, stones and traps and all, and digests them at its ease over the following days.

318.notes:
Its strongly built jaws and needle fangs pack force enough to tear the hull clean out of a boat, and it attacks in ravening schools. It cannot bear to see a wound in the water and rushes to it.
Sailors dread the churning of the water that marks a school of Carvanha, and the fisher-folk of the estuaries mend their hulls against the teeth of it.

319.notes:
Named the bully of the sea and feared the length of the coast, it is a cruel and a solitary hunter whose fangs grow back in an instant if ever they snap off. It strikes and is gone before its wake has settled.
It patrols its stretch of water alone and suffers no rival, and the pearl-divers time their dives by the hours it is known to hunt.
319.scribe: Raised from a Carvanha not by any stone, but by the plain passage of a hard and hungry youth into a harder maturity.

320.notes:
Its nostrils sit above its eyes, and it is a playful giant that loves to startle folk by snorting a great jet of seawater into the air. For all its bulk it means no harm by the game.
It fills itself with water and air to bob upon the surface, and children of the coast paddle out to a floating Wailmer as to a living island.

321.notes:
It is the largest creature yet recorded in any of the three kingdoms, and it swims the open sea with a slow and languorous grace, dwarfing the ships that pass it. It dives to depths no other beast can follow.
Sailors who meet one becalmed upon the swell speak of it ever after in hushed tones, and reckon the sight among the great wonders of the water.

322.notes:
It is so dull of wit that it does not notice a blow struck against it, yet it cannot abide hunger for even a moment and grows frantic the instant its belly is empty. Warm magma courses slow within it.
It plods along in a placid daze until it wants feeding, whereupon the placid daze gives way, briefly and comically, to alarm.

323.notes:
A true volcano burns within its body, and magma of a fearful heat courses through it, so that now and again the humps upon its back erupt in earnest. It grows short of temper in the cold.
The hill-folk read the mood of the fire-mountains in the mood of their Camerupt, and flee the valley when the creature's back begins to smoke.

324.notes:
It bores through the mountains in search of coal, and what it finds it packs into the hollows of its shell and burns to fuel itself, venting the smoke from the holes upon its back. A contented Torkoal puffs like a slow chimney.
The smiths of Hoenn keep one at the forge in place of a bellows, and feed it the poorer coal, which it burns as gladly as the best.

325.notes:
It bounces about upon its tail, and the jolting of that endless bouncing is what keeps its heart beating, so that it dares not stop for even a moment. To hold still would be the death of it.
It bounces even in its sleep, from long necessity, and a household that keeps one soon learns to sleep through the soft and ceaseless thudding.

326.notes:
By the black pearls set upon its body it swells its powers of the mind and bends a foe wholly to its will, and it must have those pearls to work its art. It dances a strange shuffling step when it is pleased.
Rob a Grumpig of its pearls and it is left near helpless, and so it guards them above all things and hides them close when it sleeps.

327.notes:
No two of them that exist in all the world are marked with the same pattern of spots, so that each is a singular creature, known apart from every other of its kind. It walks with a shaky, tottering, drunken step.
The scribes despaired of drawing its plate truly, for no one Spinda stands for the rest, and settled at last for a single fellow, with a note that all the others differ.
327.scribe: Its spots are unrepeatable. The plate shows but one of an uncountable company, no two alike.

328.notes:
It digs a sloped, bowl-shaped pit in the sand and waits at the bottom with endless patience for some unwary creature to tumble in. Its great jaws seldom let go of what they seize.
The desert-crossers learn to read the tell-tale funnels in the sand and step wide of them, for a Trapinch will hold a grip through thirst and hunger both.

329.notes:
It makes its prey swoon by loosing a keening from the swift beating of its two wings, a sound pitched below the hearing of most ears. It is but half-changed, and dreams already of the sky.
The desert nomads know its coming by an ache behind the eyes before ever they hear it, and cover their heads until the humming passes.

330.notes:
Named the spirit of the desert, it wheels above the dunes on green wings whose beating whips the sand into a veiling cloud, so that it is heard singing where it cannot be seen. It rules the wastes it haunts.
Caravans lost in a sandstorm have followed its song to water, and count the desert spirit a friend, though few have ever looked upon it clearly.

331.notes:
It dwells in the driest country, the deserts and the barren places, and looses a strong scent from its flower to draw prey near, then closes upon whatever comes. It hoards its water jealously against the sun.
It blooms but once a year, in the dead of the desert night, and the nomads who chance upon a flowering Cacnea count it a rare and fortunate sight.

332.notes:
Through the burning day it stands stock-still to spare itself the loss of a drop of moisture, and only when the desert night comes cold does it stir and hunt. It follows travelers through the dark, waiting for them to tire.
The caravans post a watch against it by night, for a Cacturne is patient past enduring, and dogs the weary until the weariest can walk no more.

333.notes:
Its wings are light and fluffy as cottony cloud, and it has no fear of people at all, but will alight upon a head or a shoulder as readily as upon a branch. It hums a soft and artless tune.
Children of the highlands wear a Swablu upon the shoulder like a living muffler, and the trusting creature seems as content with the arrangement as they.

334.notes:
It dances and wheels among the billowing clouds, and sings in a voice so pure and crystalline that any who hear it are lulled into a happy dream. Its cotton wings are near indistinguishable from the clouds it flies among.
Sailors on a still sea have heard that singing come drifting down out of an empty sky, and taken heart from it, though they never spied the singer.

335.notes:
The memory of its long feud with Seviper is written into its every cell, so that it knows its ancient enemy by instinct and needs no teaching to hate it. It dodges a strike with a supple and fluid grace.
Where the track of a Zangoose crosses that of a Seviper, the country folk expect a battle, and the two are named together in every tale of undying enmity.
335.scribe: Sworn enemy of Seviper (No. 336) down all the generations. Neither the scribes nor anyone else recalls the first cause of the quarrel.

336.notes:
It carries on a feud with Zangoose that runs back through untold generations, and the scars that cover its body are the tally of those vicious battles. It whets its bladed tail on stone before a fight.
It hates the smell of a Zangoose past all reason, and will break off any other pursuit to give chase, so old and so deep is the grudge between them.

337.notes:
It was found where a meteor had fallen, and for that some hold that it came down out of the sky upon the falling stone. It waxes and wanes in its power, they say, with the phases of the moon.
It floats silent through the night and turns a cold red eye upon whatever it passes, and the star-watchers reckon it a fragment of the moon come down to walk the earth.

338.notes:
A creature said to have fallen from space, it hangs in the air and moves without a sound, and in battle it looses the stored heat of the sun in a searing light. It pairs, in the old belief, with the moon-stone Lunatone.
Where the two are found together, the country folk say the sun and moon have come down to earth as a pair, and hold the place lucky.

339.notes:
Its whiskers serve it as a wonderful radar, feeling out the least stir in the muddy water, and it hides itself in the streambed with only those two feelers showing. Its body is slick with a slime that makes it near impossible to grasp.
Anglers who hook one wrestle with a thing like a wet rope, and as often as not it slips the grip and is gone into the mud.

340.notes:
It is fiercely territorial, and a single one will claim a whole pond for its own and drive off all comers, snapping at anything that dares the water. It bumps its head along the bottom as it swims, seeming not to mind.
When the ground trembles it is said to be a Whiscash thrashing below, and the villages by its pond take the shudder for its temper and let the water be.

341.notes:
It was first brought from foreign parts as a curiosity and a pet, and having escaped it took to the wild waters and thrived there past anyone's wish. It nips at anything that comes near its pincers.
It is a quarrelsome newcomer that has crowded out the native creatures of many a stream, and the water-keepers regard the spread of it with a wary eye.

342.notes:
It is possessed of an exceedingly violent nature that drives it to challenge every living thing it meets to battle, and other creatures shun the waters it haunts. It rules its stretch of river by naked force.
Where a Crawdaunt takes up residence the pond falls silent of all other life, for none will abide so ill-tempered a neighbor, and it is left at last to glower alone.

343.notes:
It moves about by spinning upon its single foot, and old wall-paintings show it living among people in the earliest days, so that it is plainly a creature of great antiquity. It seals its eyes and sleeps standing upright.
The diggers who uncover it in old ruins handle it with reverence, for it is older by far than any wall it is painted on.

344.notes:
The old belief holds it a doll of mud shaped by the first people and waked to life by a strange ray out of the sky, and it seals its eyes to sleep buried in the ground. It spins slowly, arms outstretched, as it moves.
Scholars dispute whether it was made or born, and the creature, sealing its many eyes, declines to settle the question for them.

345.notes:
It lived upon the sea-floor a hundred million years ago, and has been called back to life in this late age by the art of the learned, out of a stone that held its shape. It anchors itself and sways like a flower of the deep.
Restored, it waves its petal-arms in the modern shallows, a bloom from a sea that dried before the first of men, and the scholars come from far to marvel at it.
345.scribe: Called back from a hundred million years by the fossil-menders. It knew a sea that no living thing remembers.

346.notes:
It roams the ocean floor in search of food, and extends its trunk-like neck at will to seize whatever passes within reach of its swaying head. It fastens its base to a rock and lets the current bring its meals.
It is a patient hunter of the deep, older than the mountains, and it feeds now upon the small things of a sea its own kind helped to make.

347.notes:
It was regenerated from a fossil of the deep past, a primitive creature of the old warm seas, and it grips its prey fast in the great claws it bears and will not be shaken loose. It swims by beating the plates of its sides.
The fossil-menders raised it from a shard of stone, and it paddles the modern water in the shape it wore before there were eyes to see it.
347.scribe: Raised from ancient stone, as Lileep was. Between them they hold the two shapes life took in the first seas.

348.notes:
Its tough armor turns aside near any blow, and its two enormous claws may be shot out to their full reach or drawn back at will to seize and to rend. It walks the shallows on plated legs, a relic of a vanished age.
When it comes ashore to hunt, its shadow on the sand is the shadow of a creature ten thousand ages dead, and the fisher-folk give it the sea to itself.

349.notes:
Its fins are ragged and tattered from the first day of its life, and for its shabby and wretched look it is scorned and left alone by near everyone. It is among the feeblest creatures in any of the three kingdoms.
And yet the patient keeper who does not scorn it is repaid past all expectation, for a well-tended Feebas changes into a wonder, as the next entry tells.

350.notes:
It is beautiful past the telling of it, and those who look upon it are said to lose all thought of quarrel and go away with a quieted heart. It rises from the water in the calm after a storm.
That so wretched a fish should become so fair a creature is Hoenn's favorite marvel, and mothers tell it to their children as a promise about patience and about worth that is not seen at first.

351.notes:
Its very shape changes with the weather, and it has won the power to borrow the great forces of the sky to shield itself, so that it is one thing in sun and another in rain and another in hail. It answers the heavens moment by moment.
The weather-wise keep one by the window and read the coming day in the shape it wears at dawn, and are seldom far wrong.
351.scribe: It wears the weather. The plate shows its plain form; under sun, rain, and snow it takes three others besides.

352.notes:
It changes the colors of its body at will to melt into whatever surrounds it, and but for one part of it that will not change however it tries, it would vanish from sight altogether. It flicks out a long tongue to taste the air.
Hunters learn to watch for that one unchanging mark drifting against the background, for it is the only sign that a Kecleon is there at all.

353.notes:
It is drawn to feelings of jealousy and spite, and where a strong grudge festers in some human heart, there it will gather to feed. It grows and thrives on the ill will of others.
The old folk hold that to harbor a hatred is to invite a Shuppet to the door, and counsel letting a grievance go before the creature comes to batten on it.

354.notes:
It is a discarded doll that turned into a creature out of the grudge of being thrown away, and it wanders in search of the child that once cast it off. A pin driven into its body is said to work its curses.
The old wives counsel treating a worn-out doll with kindness at its end, and burying it rather than throwing it out, lest it come back one night wearing this shape.
354.scribe: Born of a cast-off doll's grudge. There is a small sadness in this plate that the scribes have not tried to soften.

355.notes:
It passes through any wall however thick, and once it has fixed upon a target it follows without rest or swerving until the night is done. It bears a single great eye that weeps a spectral flame.
It means, the old belief holds, only to carry off the fearful to some quiet place, though few who are chased by one in the dark stay to learn its intentions.

356.notes:
Its body is wholly hollow, empty as a drum, and the old accounts liken the dark within it to a pit that swallows all light and gives none back. It beckons with a slow hand to whatever it would draw in.
Those who have looked into the hollow of a Dusclops say the dark went down further than any body could hold, and did not look a second time.

357.notes:
It dwells in the tropical jungles, and about its neck grows a bunch of sweet fruit that ripens twice in the year and is good to eat. It flies on broad leaf-wings despite its bulk.
The jungle-dwellers gather its fallen fruit gratefully, and a Tropius that trusts a village will let the children pick from its very collar.

358.notes:
It makes its cries echo and swell within its own hollow body, and when it is roused to anger those cries sharpen into a keening that pierces the ear. It hangs by the suction of its head from a high branch.
The wind sets a whole grove of them chiming softly against one another, and travelers rest beneath the sound as beneath a wind of bells.

359.notes:
Every time it shows itself before people, a disaster follows close upon it, an earthquake or a great wave, and for that it is feared and driven off as a bringer of ruin. Yet it comes, the truth is, to give warning and not to cause the harm.
The wiser sort have learned to heed rather than hunt it, and a village that takes an Absol's coming as a sign to seek high ground has more than once been spared.
359.scribe: Blamed down the ages for the calamities it only foretells. This codex records it as a herald wronged, not a bringer of ruin.

360.notes:
It is seen always with a wide and happy smile, and to know its true mood one must look not to its face but to its tail. Two of them press their tails together and endure a hardship in company, seeming to find the trouble half a game.
It bounces along at its mother's side without a care, and its gladness is so plain that the sour of heart are cheered against their will.
360.scribe: The infant form of Johto's Wobbuffet (No. 202), set down at last now that the third kingdom is opened.

361.notes:
It dwells in the country of heavy snows, and in the green seasons when no snow falls it slips into houses and makes off with what food it finds. It wears a pointed hood that hides all but its glinting eyes.
The snow-country folk leave out a share of food against its coming, reckoning it cheaper to give than to be robbed, and hold a well-fed Snorunt for a lucky guest.

362.notes:
Its body is of rock, sheathed in an armor of its own ice, and it freezes the moisture of the air about it to mend and thicken that armor at need. It opens vast jaws to swallow the cold and breathe it out again.
It is said to freeze a foe where it stands with a single breath, and the mountain-folk speak of statues of ice upon the high passes that were living things but a moment before.

363.notes:
It gets about far faster by rolling than by walking on its small flippers, and when a company of them feed together they all clap their fins at once to show their gladness. It claps for near any reason, or none.
A beach of clapping Spheal is a comical din, and the coast-children clap back at them until the whole shore is applauding the tide.

364.notes:
It has a keen and questioning nose, and touches every new thing to that nose first to learn what it is, testing the world by scent before all else. It balances a ball upon that nose for the simple pleasure of it.
The show-folk of the coast train it to catch and spin whatever is tossed to it, and a Sealeo at its juggling draws a crowd on any market day.

365.notes:
Its two great tusks are grown so massive that a single blow of them will shatter a block of ice weighing ten tons, and it uses them to break through the floes to the sea beneath. It layers on blubber against the bitterest cold.
The eldest bulls bear tusks scored with the record of a hundred winters, and rule the ice-floes by the plain weight of them.

366.notes:
Its sturdy shell serves it for more than shelter, for it clamps that shell shut upon passing prey to catch it, and a full-grown Clamperl is said to hold a pearl of great price within. It shuts fast at the least alarm.
The pearl-divers prize it above all the shellfish of the reef, and a Clamperl's pearl is set in the crowns of the coastal lords.

367.notes:
It lives at so great a depth that people knew nothing of it for the longest age, and it lures prey in the black water with a tail shaped cunningly like a small fish. It bites with a mouth grown all out of proportion.
The deep-net fishers who first hauled one up took it for a monster, and the learned dispute to this day by what strange road it came to be.
367.scribe: Raised from a Clamperl by trade, while it held a Deep Sea Tooth. Its sister-form Gorebyss took the other road (No. 368).

368.notes:
It lives in the warm southern seas at a depth where the weight of the water would crush a lesser thing, and its slender body is built to bear that pressure. It draws the fluids of its prey through a fine and pointed snout.
It is a creature of rare and delicate beauty for so dark a home, and the deep-divers who glimpse its rose-colored form by lantern-light do not soon forget it.
368.scribe: Raised from a Clamperl by trade, while it held a Deep Sea Scale. Its brother-form Huntail took the other road (No. 367).

369.notes:
It has kept its shape unchanged for a hundred million years and more, a living relic of the first seas that never found need to alter. It swims slowly along the deep rock, minding its own ancient business.
The deep-net fishers hold it in a kind of awe, for it was old before the mountains rose, and they return it gently to the water when it comes up in the net.

370.notes:
It dwells in the warm shallows of the tropic seas, and it earned its name by swimming after loving couples, drawn to their happiness. Its very shape is that of a heart.
The coast-folk give a pair of Luvdisc as a token between sweethearts, and hold that where the little fish gather, love is close behind.

371.notes:
It dreams of one day soaring in the sky, and in its doomed attempts at flight it hurls itself from cliffs again and again, so that its head has grown hard as rock from the falling. It bears the bruises of its hope without complaint.
The hill-folk watch the young ones fling themselves from the crags and are half moved and half amused, for the dream will come true in the end, though not for a long while yet.

372.notes:
Within its armor-like shell its whole body is being unmade and made anew, and it holds itself still and endures while the great change works. It cracks the shell only when the new form is ready.
It bears the waiting with a stony patience, and the country folk take a Shelgon for a lesson in biding one's time until the appointed hour.

373.notes:
It came to be, the old accounts say, out of a fierce and long-held longing to grow wings, until the very longing worked a change upon its body and gave it the sky. Loosed to fly at last, it is wild with the joy of it.
It wheels and roars over the cliffs where once it could only fall, and the hill-folk keep their distance, for a Salamence drunk on flight is a danger to all beneath it.

374.notes:
It speaks with its fellows in pulses of magnetism rather than in any sound, and in a swarm they move all as one body, wheeling and turning in perfect and silent unison. It has one eye and a single fixed purpose.
A cloud of Beldum turning together in the air, no one of them a hair's breadth out of place, is a strange and a soundless marvel.

375.notes:
It is formed when two Beldum join, and their two brains are wedded by a nervous system of magnetism into a single sharper mind. It stills its own weight with magnetic force to float and to strike.
It reasons better than either of its halves alone, and the scholars watch the joining of two into one wiser with a mixture of wonder and unease.

376.notes:
Four brains in all are joined within it, and together they outrace the finest calculating engine at any reckoning, so that it fights as much by cold arithmetic as by force. It folds its four legs beneath it to fall upon a foe from above.
It claims its ground by the plain terror of its bulk and its wit both, and the smiths of Hoenn reckon its iron body worth a king's ransom, could any but subdue it.

377.notes:
It was sealed away by people in the deep past, and if its rocky body is broken in battle it is said to seek out fitting stones and fix them in place to mend itself. It moves with a slow and grinding tread.
The old seals that bound it are carved with warnings, and the diggers who break into its chamber weigh their curiosity against the wisdom of those who shut it in.
377.scribe: One of three sealed guardians of Hoenn. It was bound away for a reason the seals do not name.

378.notes:
Its body was made in the depths of an ice age, and is frozen so deep that no fire will melt it, and the cold pours off it in a killing wave. It moves with a slow and grinding chill about it.
The glacier-folk found its chamber cut in the heart of an old ice-field, and sealed it again after, judging some things better left frozen.
378.scribe: One of three sealed guardians of Hoenn, forged of the deepest cold of an elder age.

379.notes:
Its body is harder than any metal known, and hollow besides, and what fills that hollow, if anything, no one has ever learned. It bears upon it the marks of the seals that bound it long ago.
The smiths would give much to know the secret of a metal that outlasts their hardest steel, but the creature keeps its counsel, and the seals keep theirs.
379.scribe: One of three sealed guardians of Hoenn. Its metal is beyond the smiths, and its hollow beyond the scholars.

380.notes:
It is keenly alive to the feelings of the people about it, and at the least breath of hostility it bristles the down that covers its body and takes flight. It cloaks itself from sight and glides unseen through the air.
It shows itself only to the gentle, and to be befriended by a Latias is counted among the rarest fortunes in all Hoenn.
380.scribe: One of the two eon dragons, sister to Latios (No. 381). The two are seldom found apart for long.

381.notes:
It can lay upon a foe's mind an image of whatever it has seen or imagined, so that the foe cannot tell the seeming from the true. It is highly intelligent, and understands the speech of people.
It flies faster than any bird when it folds its wings to its body, and the two eon dragons racing the wind together are a sight granted to very few.
381.scribe: One of the two eon dragons, brother to Latias (No. 380). It gives its very heart, the old tale says, to shield the one it loves.

382.notes:
It has the power to raise vast rain-clouds that cover the whole sky and loose torrents upon the land, and the old myths name it the sweller of the seas. It sleeps in a trench at the bottom of the deep.
When it wakes, the rains come without end, and the coastal peoples pray it back to sleep, for the sea rises to answer its waking.
382.scribe: The old myth of the sea. It and Groudon (No. 383) are the two halves of an ancient and world-shaking quarrel.

383.notes:
The old myths name it the raiser of the land, the one that lifted the continents out of the sea and drove back the water to make dry ground for living things. It sleeps in the magma deep beneath the earth.
When it wakes, the sun blazes and the rivers fail, and the peoples of the inland pray it back to sleep, for the drought follows wherever it walks.
383.scribe: The old myth of the land. It and Kyogre (No. 382) are the two halves of an ancient and world-shaking quarrel.

384.notes:
It lived for hundreds of millions of years in the high ozone of the sky and never once came down to the ground, feeding on the meteors and the motes of the upper air. It is called upon, the myths say, to quell the quarrel of the sea and the land.
When the sweller of the seas and the raiser of the land fall to war, it descends at last out of the high sky to still them both, and only then does the world look upon it.
384.scribe: The keeper of the high air, and the peacemaker of the elder myth. It comes down only when land and sea can no longer be reconciled below.

385.notes:
The old legend holds that it will grant any wish written upon a note and tied to its head at its waking, and that it wakes but once in a thousand years, for seven days, before it sleeps again. It is a small and gentle star-creature.
The hopeful of Hoenn write their dearest wishes and keep them ready against the age of its waking, though few living will ever see the week it wakes.
385.scribe: The wish-granter that wakes once in a thousand years. This codex records the legend and makes no promises on its behalf.

386.notes:
It came to be when the substance of a creature from beyond the sky was struck by a beam of light and made to change, and the crystal at its core is the heart and the whole of it. It shifts its very shape to suit attack or defense or flight.
It fell from the void a made and altered thing, and the scholars cannot agree whether it is one creature wearing many forms or many creatures sharing one core.
386.scribe: A creature from beyond the sky, altered by human light. The last folio of the third kingdom, and the far edge of this codex.
